**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 27, verses 9–14:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, it is I, Allah﴾. The *ha'* (هاء) is an *'imad* (dummy or separating pronoun, a pronoun used to introduce a clause) according to the linguists. According to al-Suddi, it refers back to the one calling out, because Musa said: "Who is this calling to me?" It was said: ﴿Indeed, it is I, Allah﴾.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And throw down your staff﴾. There is an elided element in the verse, its implied sense being: so he threw it down, and it became a snake. ﴿And when he saw it moving as if it were a *jann*﴾. Al-Farra' said: the *jann* is a snake that is neither large nor small.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And he did not turn back﴾. There are two views concerning this.

One: he did not turn around. This is the view of Qatada. The second: he did not return. This is the view of Ibn Qutayba. Al-Zajjaj said: Ibn Qutayba said: "The people of reflection hold that it is derived from *al-'aqib* (the heel, i.e., turning on one's heels)."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾. That is: they do not fear in My presence. It was also said: the intended meaning is: in the place where revelation is sent to them, so it is as if He was alerting him that whoever Allah has granted security from His punishment through prophethood should not fear a snake.

Regarding His saying: ﴿except one who wrongs﴾, there are three views.

The first: it is a *istithna' muttasil* (connected exception), the view of al-Hasan, Qatada, and Muqatil. The meaning: except one among them who has wronged, for he should fear. Ibn Qutayba said: Allah, Exalted is He, knew that Musa felt apprehension (p-157) over his sin concerning the man whom he struck, so He said: ﴿except one who wrongs, then substitutes good after evil﴾, that is: repentance and remorse, for he should fear. ﴿And indeed, I am Forgiving, Merciful﴾.

The second: it is a *istithna' munqati'* (disconnected exception), the view of Ibn al-Sa'ib and al-Zajjaj. The meaning: but whoever wrongs, he should fear. Al-Farra' said: "*min* (مِن) is an exception from those who were excluded in the speech, as if he said: the messengers do not fear in My presence; fear is only for others, except whoever wrongs, so *min* is an exception." Ibn Jarir said: there is an elided element in the verse, its implied sense being: except whoever wrongs, then whoever wrongs and then substitutes good.

The third: that *illa* (إلا) carries the meaning of *wa* (و, "and"). It is like His saying: ﴿so that people will have no argument against you, except those who wronged among them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 150]. This was related by al-Farra' from some of the grammarians, but he did not approve of it.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, Asim al-Jahdari, and Ibn Ya'mur read: *ill-a man zalama* (أَلا مَن ظَلَمَ) with a fathah on the hamzah and a light lam.

The exegetes have two views on what is meant by *zulm* (wrongdoing) here.

One: sins. The second: polytheism. The meaning of *hasanan* (حسناً, "good") is: repentance and remorse.

Ibn Mas'ud, al-Dahhak, Abu Raja', al-A'mash, Ibn al-Sumayfa', and Abd al-Warith on the authority of Abu Amr read: *hasanan* with a fathah on the *ha'* and the *sin*. ﴿After evil﴾, that is: after wrongdoing. It was said: the indication of this is that Musa, although he had wronged himself by killing the Copt, Allah will forgive him, because he regretted that and repented.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And put your hand into your pocket﴾. The *jayb* (جيب) is the opening of a shirt where it is cut open. Ibn Jarir said: He only commanded him to put his hand into his pocket because at that time he was wearing a woolen cloak that had no sleeves. The *su'* (سوء) is leprosy (*baras*).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿among nine signs﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: *fi* (في) is connected to His saying: ﴿throw down your staff﴾ and ﴿put your hand﴾. So the interpretation is: make these two manifest among nine signs. *Fi* here carries the meaning of *min* (مِن, "from"), so its interpretation is: from among nine signs. You say: "Take for me ten camels, among them two stallions," meaning: from them there are two stallions. We have explained the signs in (Bani Isra'il: 101).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿to Pharaoh and his people﴾. That is: sent to Pharaoh and his people. That was omitted because it is well known. ﴿And when Our signs came to them clearly visible﴾, that is: clear and evident. This is like His saying: ﴿And We gave Thamud the she-camel as a visible sign﴾ [al-Isra': 59]. We have explained it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They said: this﴾, that is: this which we see plainly, ﴿is clear magic﴾. ﴿And they rejected them﴾, that is: they denied them, ﴿while their souls were convinced of them﴾ that they were from Allah, ﴿out of wrongdoing﴾, that is: polytheism, ﴿and arrogance﴾, that is: haughtiness. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: they rejected them out of wrongdoing and arrogance, that is, out of pride in not believing in what Musa brought, while they knew that it was from Allah.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 27, verses 20–26:**

Allah's words: ﴿He inspected the birds﴾. *Al-tafaqqud* means seeking what has gone missing from you. The meaning is that he sought the birds that were missing from him. *Al-tayr* (birds) is a collective noun for the species. The birds used to accompany Sulayman on his journeys, shading him with their wings. ﴿He said, "Why do I not see the hoopoe?"﴾ Ibn Kathir, 'Asim and al-Kisa'i read *mā liya lā arā al-hudhhuda* with a fatha on the *yā'* (*liya*). Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah read it with a sukun on the *yā'*. The meaning is: "What is wrong with the hoopoe, that I do not see it?" The Arabs say *mā lī arāka kaʾīban*, meaning "What is wrong with you, that I see you dejected?" This is an example of *al-maqlūb* (inverted construction, a grammatical device in which the sequence of words is reversed), whose meaning is well known.

The exegetes said: When Sulayman departed from the Valley of the Ants and came to a barren stretch of land, the army became thirsty and asked him for water. The hoopoe used to guide him to water. When he said to it, "Here is water," the devils would split the rock and gush forth springs before they pitched their tents. The hoopoe could see water beneath the earth as one sees water in a glass. On that day he sought it but did not find it.

Some of them said: He sought it only because the birds used to shade them from the sun, and the hoopoe left its place open, so the sun shone upon them through the gap.

Allah's words: ﴿Or was he among the absent?﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: Its meaning is "Rather, he was among the absent."

Allah's words: ﴿I will surely punish him with a severe punishment﴾. There are six opinions on this.

The first is plucking out its feathers. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, and by the majority. The second is plucking its feathers and exposing it to the sun. This was said by 'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad. The third is tying its leg and exposing it to the sun. This was said by al-Dahhak. The fourth is smearing it with tar and exposing it to the sun. This was said by Muqatil ibn Hayyan. The fifth is confining it in a cage. The sixth is separating it from its mate. Al-Tha'labi related these last two.

Allah's words: ﴿Or he must bring me a clear authority﴾. Ibn Kathir read *la-ya'tiyannīnī* with two nūns, and so it is written in their copies of the Qur'an. As for *al-sultān*, it means proof. It was also said that it means excuse.

It is mentioned in the tafsir (exegesis) that when Sulayman halted during part of his journey, the hoopoe said: "He has busied himself with the halt. I will rise up to the sky and look at the length and breadth of the world." So it rose, and saw a garden belonging to Bilqis. It inclined toward the greenery and landed in it, and there it met another hoopoe. It asked, "From where have you come?" The other replied, "From Syria, with my master Sulayman. And where are you from?" It answered, "From this land. Its king is a woman called Bilqis. Will you come with me so that you may see her kingdom?" The hoopoe said, "I fear that Sulayman will look for me at prayer time when he needs water." The other said, "Your master would be pleased for you to bring him news of this queen." So it went with it, and saw Bilqis and her kingdom.

Ibn 'Abbas, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, al-Hasan, al-Zuhri, Qatadah, Abu al-'Aliyah, Humayd al-A'raj, al-A'mash, Ibn Abi 'Ablah and al-Kisa'i read *allā yasjudū* with a light (unshaddahed) *allā*, meaning: "Ah, O you people, prostrate!" In this reading, the word *hā'ulā'* (these) is understood and *yā* alone is retained. The pause is at *allā yā* and the beginning is *usjudū*. Al-Farra' said: On this reading it is a prostration verse, but on the reading of the one who doubles the *lām*, it should not be a prostration verse.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: This is a new command from Allah, meaning: "Ah, O people, prostrate!" Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy read *hallā yasjudū* with a *hā'*.

Allah's words: ﴿The One who brings forth what is hidden in the heavens and the earth﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: That is, what is concealed within them. It derives from *khabba'tu al-shay'*, meaning I concealed the thing. It is said: The *khab'* of the heavens is rain, and the *khab'* of the earth is plants. Al-Zajjaj said: Everything you conceal is *khab'*, so *al-khab'* is everything that is hidden. The meaning is: He knows the unseen in the heavens and the earth. Ibn Jarir said: *Fī* here means *min* (from), so the sense is: He brings forth what is hidden from the heavens.

Allah's words: ﴿And He knows what you conceal and what you declare﴾. Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, and al-Kisa'i read both verbs with the *tā'* (*tukhfūna* and *tu'linūna*). The rest read them with the *yā'*. Ibn Zayd said: From His words *"I have comprehended"* up to His words *"the Mighty"* is the speech of the hoopoe. Al-Dahhak and Ibn Muhayṣin read *al-ʿaẓīmu* with a ḍammah on the *mīm*.

(p-167) When the hoopoe finished speaking, [Solomon] said: ﴿We will see whether you have told the truth or whether you are one of the liars.﴾ He doubted his report because the hoopoe had denied that anyone else in the land had authority. Then he wrote a letter, sealed it with his ring, and gave it to the hoopoe, saying: ﴿Take this letter of mine and throw it to them.﴾ Ibn Kathir, Ibn Amir, and al-Kisa'i read "fa-alqihi-y" (فَألْقِهِي) with a connected yā' (ي). Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Abu Ja'far, and Hamza read "fa-alqihi" (فَألْقِهِ) with the ha' (ه) sukun. Qalun, transmitting from Nafi', read the ha' with a kasra without lengthening it. The meaning is: to the people of Sheba. ﴿Then withdraw from them﴾ has two interpretations. The first is: turn away. The second is: go back. ﴿And see what they return with﴾ means: what answer they send back.

The second is that the sentence contains inversion, and its sense is: see what they return with, then withdraw from them. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

Muqatil said: he carried it in his beak until he stood over the woman's head and hovered for a while while the people watched. She raised her head, and the letter was dropped into her lap. When she saw the seal, she trembled and submitted, and those of her soldiers with her also submitted.

The scholars differed over why she called it "noble" (karīm), and gave seven opinions.
First: because it was sealed. This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas.
Second: because she thought it came from God, Mighty and Majestic. This is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

Fifth: that it was awe-inspiring. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi mentioned this.
Sixth: because the hoopoe had been subjected to carry it. Al-Mawardi related this.
Seventh: because she saw in its opening "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful." Al-Tha'labi related this.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 27, verse 32–35:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Advise me in my affair﴾, meaning: explain to me what I should do, and give me your counsel. Al-Farra' said: "She made counsel into fatwa (ruling), and that is permissible because of the breadth of the language."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿I would not decide a matter﴾, meaning: I would not carry it out, ﴿until you witness﴾, meaning: until you attend; the sense is: not except with your presence and your counsel.

﴿They said: We are men of great strength﴾. Regarding this there are two views.

One: they meant strength of bodies. The second: abundance of numbers, valour and courage in war.

Regarding what they intended by that saying, there are two views. One: the handing over of the matter to her opinion. The second: an indirect offer from them to fight if she commands them.

Then they said: ﴿And the command is yours﴾, meaning: in fighting and in not fighting. ﴿She said: Indeed, when kings enter a town﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: when they enter it by force, by war and conquest.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They corrupt it﴾, meaning: they ruin it, ﴿and make the honoured of its people abased﴾, meaning: they humiliate its nobles so that their rule may be secure. The sense of the speech is that she was warning them of Sulayman's march against them and his entering their lands.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And thus they do﴾. Regarding this there are two views.

One: that it is from God Exalted's confirmation of her words; this is said by al-Zajjaj.

The second: that it is part of her speech; the meaning being: "Thus Sulayman and his companions do when they enter our lands," related by al-Mawardi.

(p-170) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed I am sending them a gift﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: the gift was sent so that she might know whether he was a prophet, who would not desire worldly things, or a king, who would be pleased with the present. She sent three bricks of gold, each brick weighing one hundred ratl; a red ruby a span long, pierced; thirty male servants and thirty female servants; and she dressed them all in one garment so that the male could not be distinguished from the female. Then she wrote to him: "I have sent you a gift, so accept it. I have sent you a ruby a span long; insert a thread into it and seal both ends of the thread with your ring. I have sent you thirty male servants and thirty female servants; distinguish between the slave-girls and the boys." The chief of the devils came to him and informed him of what she had sent. He said to him: "Go and spread out, on the road of the people from the gate of my assembly, eight miles by eight miles, bricks of gold." So he went, and the devils cut the bricks from the mountains, gilded them with gold, spread them out, and set up along the road pillars of red ruby. When the envoys came, some of them said to others: "How will you enter upon this man with three bricks, when he has what you have seen?" Their leader said: "We are only envoys." So they entered upon him, and placed the bricks before him. He said: "Will you supply me with wealth?" Then he called for an ant, tied a thread to it, and passed it through the hole of the ruby until it came out of its other end; then he joined the two ends of the thread, sealed it, and handed it back to them. Then he distinguished between the boys and the girls. All of this is related from Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: she made the clothing of the boys for the girls and the clothing of the girls for the boys, so he distinguished them and did not accept her gift.

(p-171) Regarding the number of the female and male servants there are five views.

One: thirty male servants and thirty female servants, which we have mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: five hundred boys and five hundred girls, said by Wahb. The third: two hundred boys and two hundred girls, said by Mujahid. The fourth: ten boys and ten girls, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The fifth: one hundred male servants and one hundred female servants, said by Muqatil.

Regarding the means by which he distinguished them there are three views.

One: that he commanded them to perform ablution; the boy began from his elbow to his palm, and the girl began from her palm to her elbow, and he distinguished them by that. This is said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The second: that the boys began washing the backs of the forearms before their palms, and the girls the reverse; said by Qatada.

The third: that the boy scooped with his hand, and the girl poured water over her hand; said by al-Suddi.

It has come in the tafsir that she commanded the slave-girls to speak to Sulayman with the speech of men, and commanded the men to speak to him with the speech of women; and she sent a cup asking him to fill it with water that is neither from the sky nor from the water of the earth. So he caused the horses to run, and filled it with their sweat.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So shall I wait and see with what the messengers return﴾, meaning: with acceptance or with rejection.

Ibn Jarir said: the origin of "bima" is "bima" (with what), and the alif was dropped because when the Arabs use "ma" with the meaning of "ay" (which) and then join it to a preposition, they drop its alif, to distinguish between the interrogative and the declarative, as in His saying: ﴿About what do they question one another?﴾ [al-Naba': 1] and ﴿They said: In what state were you?﴾ [al-Nisa': 97]. Perhaps they retain the alif in it, as the poet said:

(p-172) "'Ala ma qama yashtumuna la'imun / kakhinzirin tamarraga fi ramad?"

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 27, verse 32–35:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Advise me in my affair﴾, meaning: explain to me what I should do, and give me your counsel. Al-Farra' said: "She made counsel into fatwa (ruling), and that is permissible because of the breadth of the language."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿I would not decide a matter﴾, meaning: I would not carry it out, ﴿until you witness﴾, meaning: until you attend; the sense is: not except with your presence and your counsel.

﴿They said: We are men of great strength﴾. Regarding this there are two views.

One: they meant strength of bodies. The second: abundance of numbers, valour and courage in war.

Regarding what they intended by that saying, there are two views. One: the handing over of the matter to her opinion. The second: an indirect offer from them to fight if she commands them.

Then they said: ﴿And the command is yours﴾, meaning: in fighting and in not fighting. ﴿She said: Indeed, when kings enter a town﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: when they enter it by force, by war and conquest.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They corrupt it﴾, meaning: they ruin it, ﴿and make the honoured of its people abased﴾, meaning: they humiliate its nobles so that their rule may be secure. The sense of the speech is that she was warning them of Sulayman's march against them and his entering their lands.

One: that it is from God Exalted's confirmation of her words; this is said by al-Zajjaj.

The second: that it is part of her speech; the meaning being: "Thus Sulayman and his companions do when they enter our lands," related by al-Mawardi.

The Qur'an reading "﴿فَلَمّا جاءَ سُلَيْمانَ﴾" (When he came to Solomon). Al-Zajjaj said: "When his messenger came to him." It is also possible that it means: "When his kindness (birr) came to him."

The Qur'an reading "﴿أتُمِدُّونَنِ بِمالٍ﴾" (Will you supply me with wealth?). Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "أتُمِدُّونَنِي" with two nuns and a yā' in pause and in continuation. Al-Musayyibi related from Nafi': "أتُمِدُّونِي" with one light nun and a yā' in both continuation and pause. ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir and al-Kisa'i read "أتُمِدُّونَنِ" without a yā' in both continuation and pause. Hamzah read "أتُمِدُّونِي بِمالٍ" with one doubled (shaddah) nun and stopping on the yā'.

The Qur'an reading "﴿فَما آتانِيَ اللَّهُ﴾" (What Allah has given me). Ibn Kathir, Ibn ʿĀmir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from ʿĀṣim read "فَما آَتانِ اللَّهُ" with a kasrah on the nun and no yā'. Abu 'Amr, Nafi' and Hafs from ʿĀṣim read "آتانِيَ" with a fatḥah on the yā'. All of them read the tā' with a fatḥah except al-Kisa'i, who inclined it (imālah) in "آتانِيَ اللَّهُ". Hamzah inclined "أنا آَتِيكَ بِهِ" and pronounced the nun with a slight trace of kasrah. The meaning is: "What Allah has given me," that is, of prophethood and kingship, "is better than what He has given you," that is, of wealth. "Rather, you rejoice in your gift" means: when one of you sends a gift to another, he rejoices, but as for me, I do not. Then he said to the messenger: "﴿Return to them, for we shall surely come to them with hosts that they cannot withstand﴾," that is, that they have no power against, "﴿and we shall surely drive them out from there﴾," meaning from their land.

When her messengers returned to her with the news, she said: "I know that it is not a kingdom, and we have no power against it." So she sent to him: "I am sending to you with the nobles of my people, to see what he calls to." Then she ordered her throne to be placed behind seven doors and assigned guards to protect it. She set out to Solomon with twelve thousand commanders, each commander having thousands under him. Solomon was awe-inspiring and would not begin anything until he was asked about it. One day he sat on the throne of his kingdom and saw a dust cloud near him. He said: "What is this?" They said: "Bilqis has arrived at this place," and it was a farsakh away. He had been told that she had secured her throne before leaving. So ﴿he said: "O chiefs, which of you will bring me her throne?"﴾ There are five opinions about his reason for seeking it.

The first: so that he would know the truth of the hoopoe. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: to make it a proof of the truth of his prophethood, because she had left it in her house and secured it, and he found that it had gone ahead of her. This was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih.

The third: to test her intelligence and understanding, whether she would recognize it or deny it. This was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

The fourth: because its description pleased him, and he feared that she would embrace Islam, and then her wealth would be forbidden to him, so he wanted to take it before that. This was said by Qatadah.

The fifth: to show her the power of Allah the Exalted and the greatness of His dominion. This was related by al-Thaʿlabi.

The Qur'an: ﴿A ʿifrit from the jinn said﴾. Abu ʿUbaydah said: the ʿifrit is, among any jinn or human, the one who is outstanding, exaggerating in leadership. Ibn Qutaybah said: the ʿifrit is the strong and firm one.

Al-Zajjaj said: the ʿifrit is one who is decisive in the matter, exaggerating in it, along with wickedness and cunning.

Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, al-Ḍaḥḥak, Abu al-ʿĀliyah, Ibn Yaʿmur, and ʿĀṣim al-Jahdari read "قالَ عَفْرِيتٌ" with a fatḥah on the ʿayn and a kasrah on the rāʾ. Ibn Abi Shurayh related from al-Kisa'i: "عِفْرِيَةٌ" with a fatḥah on the yā' and lightened; it is also related from him that it was doubled, with tanwin on the hā' as a feminine form. Ibn Masʿud and Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ read "عِفْراةٌ" with a kasrah on the ʿayn, a fatḥah on the rāʾ, and an alif without a yā'.

The Qur'an: ﴿before you rise from your place﴾, that is, from your assembly. Similar is ﴿in a secure place﴾ [al-Dukhan: 51]. Solomon used to sit to judge between the people from the time of dawn until sunrise. It was also said: until midday. ﴿And indeed I am strong for it﴾, that is, for carrying it, ﴿trustworthy﴾.

Regarding His words ﴿trustworthy﴾ there are two opinions.

The first: trustworthy over what is in it of jewels, pearls and other things. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The second: trustworthy that I will not bring you anything else in its place. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

Solomon said: "I want it faster than that." ﴿The one who had knowledge from the Scripture said﴾. Was he a human or an angel? There are two opinions.

The first: he was human. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Ḍaḥḥak and Abu Salih. Then there are four opinions. The first: he was a man from the Children of Israel, named Asaf ibn Barkhiya. This was said by Muqatil. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Asaf, who used to stand at Solomon's head with a sword, called out, so Allah sent the angels, who carried the throne beneath the earth, digging through the earth, until the earth split open with the throne before Solomon's eyes.

The second: it was Solomon himself, peace be upon him, but a man had said to him: "I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you." He said: "Bring it." The man said: "You are the prophet, son of a prophet. If you call on Allah, it will come to you." So he called on Allah and it came to him. This was said by Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir.

The third: it was al-Khiḍr. This was said by Ibn Lahiʿah.

The fourth: it was a worshipper who had come out that day from an island in the sea, found Solomon, prayed, and so the throne was brought. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The second opinion: he was one of the angels. Then there are two opinions. The first: it was Jibril, peace be upon him. The second: it was an angel whom Allah strengthened Solomon with. Al-Thaʿlabi related both opinions.

Regarding the knowledge he had from the Scripture there are three opinions.

The first: it is the Greatest Name of Allah. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, and the majority.

The second: it is the knowledge of Solomon's letter to Bilqis.

The third: it is the knowledge of what Allah wrote for the children of Adam. This, according to the view that he was an angel, was related by al-Mawardi, who reported both opinions.

Regarding His words ﴿before your glance returns to you﴾ there are four opinions.

The first: before the farthest thing you look at comes to you. This was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

The second: before your glance ends when you extend it to its limit. This was said by Wahb.

The third: before your glance returns exhausted when you keep looking continuously. This was said by Mujahid.

The fourth: in the time it takes to open your eye and then blink. This was said by al-Zajjaj. Mujahid said: he prayed and said: "O Possessor of Majesty and Honor." Ibn al-Sa'ib said: he only said: "O Living, O Self-Subsisting."

The Qur'an: ﴿When he saw it﴾. There is an omitted part in the speech; its estimation is: so he called on Allah, [and it was brought] to him, and when he saw it, meaning Solomon, ﴿settled beside him﴾, that is, firmly established before him. ﴿He said: "This is﴾, meaning: the empowerment to attain what is sought.

The first: "Shall I give thanks for the throne, since you have brought it, or shall I be ungrateful when I see someone lower than me in this world who is more knowledgeable than me?" This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: "Shall I give thanks for this as a favor of Allah upon me, or shall I be ungrateful to His blessing by not giving thanks to Him?" This was said by Ibn Jarir.

The first: it is the Greatest Name of Allah. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, and the majority.

The second: it is the knowledge of Solomon's letter to Bilqis.

The third: it is the knowledge of what Allah wrote for the children of Adam. This, according to the view that he was an angel, was related by al-Mawardi, who reported both opinions.

Regarding His words ﴿before your glance returns to you﴾ there are four opinions.

The first: before the farthest thing you look at comes to you. This was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

The second: before your glance ends when you extend it to its limit. This was said by Wahb.

The third: before your glance returns exhausted when you keep looking continuously. This was said by Mujahid.

The fourth: in the time it takes to open your eye and then blink. This was said by al-Zajjaj. Mujahid said: he prayed and said: "O Possessor of Majesty and Honor." Ibn al-Sa'ib said: he only said: "O Living, O Self-Subsisting."

The Qur'an: ﴿When he saw it﴾. There is an omitted part in the speech; its estimation is: so he called on Allah, [and it was brought] to him, and when he saw it, meaning Solomon, ﴿settled beside him﴾, that is, firmly established before him. ﴿He said: "This is﴾, meaning: the empowerment to attain what is sought.

The Qur'an: ﴿Do I give thanks or am I ungrateful?﴾ There are two opinions.

The first: "Shall I give thanks for the throne, since you have brought it, or shall I be ungrateful when I see someone lower than me in this world who is more knowledgeable than me?" This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: "Shall I give thanks for this as a favor of Allah upon me, or shall I be ungrateful to His blessing by not giving thanks to Him?" This was said by Ibn Jarir.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 27, verses 41–44:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He said, "Disguise her throne for her"﴾. The exegetes (mufassirun) said: The devils feared that Sulayman would marry Bilqis, and she would reveal to him the secrets of the jinn, because her mother had been a jinn. Then they would no longer be subjugated to Sulayman and his descendants after him. So they spoke ill of her and said: "There is something wrong with her intellect, and her leg is like a donkey's hoof." Sulayman wished to test her intellect by disguising her throne, and to look at her feet through the building of the palace (al-sarh). Ibn Qutayba said: The meaning of ﴿nakkirū﴾ is "change it." It is said: "I disguised (nakkartu) the thing, so it became disguised (tanakkara)," meaning I changed it, so it changed.

The exegetes differed on how it was changed, with six opinions.

The first: It was added to and subtracted from. This was narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas.

The second: They made the gold plates that were on it into silver plates, and the silver plates into gold plates; the rubies in place of the emeralds, and the pearls in place of the lulu; and the two legs of emerald in place of the two legs of ruby. This was also said by Ibn Abbas.

The third: They removed from it its gems and jewels. This was also narrated from Ibn Abbas.

The fourth: They made what was red green, and what was green red. This was said by Mujahid.

The fifth: They made its bottom its top, and its front its back, and they added to it and subtracted from it. This was said by Qatada.

The sixth: They made in it images of fish. This was said by Abu Salih.

Regarding His saying: ﴿as if it were it﴾, there are two opinions.

One: When she saw it, she began to recognize it and to deny it. Then she said to herself: "How could it reach that, while it is in seven rooms with guards around it?" Then she said: "As if it were it." This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. Qatada said: She likened it to her throne. al-Suddi said: She found in it what she recognized, so she did not deny it, and she found in it what she denied, so she did not affirm it. That is why she said: "As if it were it."

The second: She recognized it, but she made it ambiguous for them just as they had made it ambiguous for her. For if they had said, "This is your throne," she would have said, "Yes." This was said by Muqatil. The exegetes said: It was said to her, "Indeed it is your throne," and the closing of the doors did not avail her anything.

Regarding His saying: ﴿and we were given the knowledge﴾, there are three opinions.

The first: It is the saying of Sulayman. This was said by Mujahid. Then, regarding its meaning, there are two opinions. One: "We were given knowledge of Allah and His power to do what He wills, through this woman." The second: "We were given knowledge of her Islam and her coming submissively, before her coming, and we were Muslims to Allah."

The second opinion: It is from the saying of Bilqis. When she saw her throne, she said: "I have recognized this sign, and we were given the knowledge of the truth of Sulayman's prophethood through the earlier signs," meaning the matter of the hoopoe and the messengers sent before this verse, "and we were Muslims, submitting to your command before we came."

The third: It is from the saying of the people of Sulayman. This was related by al-Mawardi.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And what she used to worship besides Allah had kept her back﴾. al-Farra' said: The meaning of the speech is: she was intelligent, but what kept her from worshipping Allah was her worship of the sun and the moon, which was a custom from the religion of her fathers. The meaning is: what she used to worship kept her from worshipping Allah. He said: It has been said: "Sulayman kept her back," meaning he prevented her from what she used to worship. al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: the custom she had been upon kept her from faith, because she had grown up knowing only a people who worshipped the sun. Her worship is explained by His saying: ﴿Indeed, she was of a disbelieving people.﴾ Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Abi Abla read "annahā kānat" with a fathah on the hamzah.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿It was said to her, "Enter the palace."﴾ The exegetes said: He commanded the devils, and they built for him a palace (sarh) in the form of a terrace, of glass.

Regarding the reason for his commanding that, there are three opinions.

One: He wished to show her a king who is mightier than her king. This was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih.

The second: He wished to look at her leg without asking her to uncover it, because he had been told that her leg was like a donkey's hoof. So he commanded that a house of glass be prepared for her above the water, and he placed Sulayman's throne in the middle of the house. This is the saying of Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi.

The third: He did this to test her, just as she had tested him with the female and male servants. This was mentioned by Ibn Jarir.

As for the palace (al-sarh), Ibn Qutayba said: It is the castle, and its plural is ṣurūḥ. From it is the saying of the Hudhali poet:

"Along roads like the necks of camels, their landmarks seem to them to be palaces."

He said: It is also said: the sarh is a paved floor made for her of glass, with water and fish placed beneath it.

Mujahid said: It was a pool of water over which Sulayman placed glass. Muqatil said: It was a palace of glass built over the water, with fish beneath it.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿She thought it was a pool﴾, which is the main body of water, ﴿and she uncovered her shins﴾ because of the entering of the water. Then Sulayman called to her: ﴿Indeed, it is a palace made smooth﴾, meaning made smooth and slippery, ﴿of glass﴾, meaning of crystal. Then she knew at that moment that the kingdom of Sulayman was from Allah, the Exalted, and she said: ﴿My Lord, I have wronged myself﴾, meaning by worshipping other than You. It was said: She had assumed of Sulayman that he intended to drown her in the water, so when she knew that it was a palace made smooth, she said: "My Lord, I have wronged myself by that assumption, and I have submitted with Sulayman." Then Sulayman married her. It was also said: He returned her to her kingdom, and he would visit her once a month and stay with her three days, and she bore him a child. It was also said: He married her to one of the kings, and he did not marry her himself.

The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 27, verses 48–53:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And there were in the city﴾ — meaning al-Hijr, where Salih had settled — ﴿nine men who spread corruption in the land﴾. He means: in the land of al-Hijr. Their corruption was their disbelief and their acts of disobedience. They used to shed blood and assault wealth and chastity, and they were the ones who took part in killing the she-camel. It is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah that they said: their corruption was breaking dirhams and dinars. ﴿They said﴾ among themselves, ﴿Swear to one another by Allah﴾, that is: swear by Allah, ﴿that we will surely attack him﴾, that is: we will surely kill Salih, ﴿and his family﴾ by night, ﴿then we will surely say﴾. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "latubayyitannahu wa-ahlahu thumma lataqulunna" with the ta' in both places. Mujahid, Abu Raja' and Humayd ibn Qays read "layubayyitannahu" with a ya' and a ta' both marked with damma, "thumma layaqulunna" with a ya' marked with fatha, a qaf marked with damma, a waw sakin and a lam marked with damma. ﴿To his guardian﴾, that is: to the guardian of his blood, if he asks us about him: ﴿We did not witness﴾, that is: we were not present, ﴿the destruction of his family﴾. Most readers read "mahlika" with a damma on the mim and a fatha on the lam. The word mahlik may be a verbal noun meaning the act of destroying, or it may be a place. Abu Bakr and Aban, from 'Asim, transmitted it with a fatha on the mim and the lam, meaning the destruction; it is said: halaka yahlaku mahlakan. Hafs and al-Mufaddal transmitted from him a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the lam, which is the noun of place, meaning: we did not witness the place of their destruction. So this was their scheme, and Allah repaid them for it and destroyed them.

Regarding the manner of their destruction there are four opinions.

The first: they came to the house of Salih with drawn swords, and the angels pelted them with stones and killed them. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: Allah struck them with a rock and they were killed. This is said by Qatadah.

The third: they entered a cave awaiting the coming of Salih, and Allah sent a rock that sealed the mouth of the cave. This is said by Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: they descended at the foot of a mountain, some waiting for others in order to go to the house of Salih, and the mountain fell upon them and destroyed them. This is said by Muqatil.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That We destroyed them﴾. 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "annaa dammarnahum" with a fatha on the alif. Others read it with a kasra. Whoever reads with a kasra makes it a new sentence. Whoever reads with a fatha, Abu 'Ali said: there are two possibilities.

One: that it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿the outcome of their scheme﴾.

Two: that it is governed by an implied subject, as if he said: it is that We destroyed them.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So those are their houses, fallen in ruin﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal); the meaning is: look at their houses, fallen in ruin.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 27, verse 54–58:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Do you indeed approach immorality while you see?﴾ Regarding this there are two opinions.

One of them: "while you know that it is immorality." The second: "and some of you see others."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Rather, you are a people who are ignorant.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: "You are ignorant of the Resurrection and the outcome of disobedience."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿We destined it to be among those who remained behind.﴾ That is: We made it, by Our decree and Our judgment, among those who remained behind in the punishment. Abu Bakr, on the authority of Asim, recited "qadarnaha" (with a light qaf and dal), and it carries the meaning of the emphasized form. The rest of the story has already been explained [Hud: 77].

**Ibn al-Jawzi's commentary (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 27, verses 59–61:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "All praise is for Allah"﴾. This is an address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who was commanded to praise Allah for the destruction of the disbelieving nations. It was also said: for all His blessings. ﴿And peace be upon His servants whom He has chosen﴾. Regarding them there are four opinions.

The first: they are the Messengers. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. Ikrimah also narrated from him, saying: He chose Ibrahim with (divine) friendship (al-khullah), Musa with speech, and Muhammad with vision.

(p-185) The second: they are the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). This was narrated by Abu Malik from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Suddi also said this.

The third: they are those who affirmed His oneness and believed in Him. This was narrated by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: it is Muhammad (ﷺ). This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is Allah better, or what they associate (with Him)?﴾ Abu 'Ubaydah said: its majaz (figurative or elliptical sense) is: "Or what they associate?" This is an address to the polytheists, and the meaning is: Is Allah better for the one who worships Him, or are the idols better for their worshippers?! The sense of the speech is that, after He related to them the stories of the earlier nations, He informed them that He saved those who worshipped Him, and the idols did not avail them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or who created the heavens﴾. Its implied sense is: "Is what they associate better, or who created the heavens ﴿and the earth, and sent down for you water from the sky, and We caused to grow thereby gardens of delightful beauty﴾?!" As for "hada'iq" (gardens), Ibn Qutaybah said: they are orchards, singular "hadiqah," named so because it is enclosed around (yuhdiqu 'alayha), i.e., fenced in. And "bahjah" means beauty.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It was not for you to cause its trees to grow﴾. That is: it is not befitting for you to do that, [because] you are not able to do it. Then He said, questioning them in denunciation: ﴿Is there a god with Allah?﴾ That is: there is no god with Him (p-186) ﴿Rather, they are a people who ascribe equals (to Allah)﴾, meaning the disbelievers of Makkah. We have explained this at the beginning of Surah (al-An'am). ﴿Or who made the earth a place of stability﴾, that is, a settled resting place that does not shake its inhabitants, ﴿and placed within it rivers﴾, that is, between its parts, ﴿and placed upon it firm mountains﴾, that is, fixed mountains, ﴿and placed between the two seas a barrier﴾, that is, a barrier from His power preventing the sweet and the salt from mixing. ﴿Rather, most of them do not know﴾ the extent of the greatness of Allah.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 27, verse 62–75:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Is not He who answers the distressed one (al-mudtarr)﴾ when he calls upon Him, [al-mudtarr being] the one who is afflicted and exhausted; ﴿and removes the evil﴾, meaning the harm; ﴿and makes you successors (khulafa') of the earth﴾, that is, He destroys one generation and brings forth others. And ﴿you remember (tadhakkarun)﴾ means you take heed. Abu 'Amr read it with the yaʼ (yatadhakkarun), and the rest read it with the taʼ.

﴿Or who guides you﴾, that is, directs you to your destinations when you travel, ﴿in the darknesses of the land and the sea﴾. We have explained this in (al-An'am: 63, 97), and we have explained the words that follow it in what has passed (al-A'raf: 57 and Yunus: 4), up to His saying: ﴿and they do not perceive﴾, meaning those in the heavens and the earth, ﴿when they will be raised (ayyana yub'athun)﴾, that is, when they will be raised after their death.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Rather, their knowledge has followed up (idarak) concerning the Hereafter﴾. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read: "bal adraka (rather, it has overtaken)". Mujahid said: "bal" here has the meaning of "am" (or), and the meaning is: their knowledge has not overtaken it. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is: "Has their knowledge overtaken the knowledge of the Hereafter?" On this reading the meaning is that they do not, in this world, stand upon the reality of knowledge of the Hereafter. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read: ﴿bal idarak﴾, with the meaning "bal tadarak", that is, it followed closely and came in succession, so the taʼ was assimilated into the dal. Then there are two opinions regarding its meaning.

One: their knowledge will be perfected on the Day of Resurrection because they will be raised; this was said by al-Zajjaj. Ibn 'Abbas said: what they were ignorant of in the world, they will know in the Hereafter.

The second: their conjecture and guesswork about the Hereafter has followed one another; at times they say it will occur, and at times they say it will not occur; this was said by Ibn Qutaybah. Abu Bakr narrated from 'Asim: "bal iddara'a", on the pattern of ifta'ala from adraktu.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Rather, they are in doubt about it﴾, that is, rather, today they are in doubt about the Resurrection. ﴿Rather, they are blind concerning it﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, blind to its knowledge. What follows has already been explained (al-Nahl: 127; al-Mu'minun: 35, 82), up to His saying: ﴿When is this promise?﴾, meaning the punishment with which you threaten us. ﴿Say: "Perhaps some of what you seek to hasten has drawn near to you (radifa lakum)"﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: it has drawn near to you. Ibn Qutaybah said: it has followed you, and the lam is extra, as if He said: radifakum.

Regarding what followed them of what they sought to hasten, there are two opinions.

One: the Day of Badr. The second: the punishment of the grave.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is full of bounty toward mankind﴾. Muqatil said: toward the people of Makkah, in that He does not hasten the punishment upon them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows what their breasts conceal﴾, that is, what they hide, ﴿and what they reveal﴾ by their tongues of enmity and opposition toward you. The meaning is that He will recompense them for it.

﴿And there is not an unseen thing in the heaven or earth﴾, that is, there is not any unseen matter, ﴿but that it is in a clear record (kitab)﴾, meaning the Preserved Tablet. The meaning is: the knowledge of what they seek to hasten of punishment is clear with Allah, even if it is hidden from creation.

(p. 190) **﴿Indeed, this Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel﴾.** This was because the People of the Book differed among themselves and became factions, each one attacking the other. So the Qur'an was revealed to explain what they had disagreed about, and had they followed it, they would have been safe. **﴿Indeed, your Lord will judge between them﴾**, meaning between the Children of Israel, **﴿by His judgment﴾**. Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu ʿImran al-Jawni and ʿAsim al-Jahdari recited "bi-ḥukmihi" with a kasra on the ḥa' and a fatḥa on the kaf.

Allah the Exalted says: **﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾**. The commentators said: this is a parable that Allah struck for the disbelievers, comparing them to the dead.

Allah the Exalted says: **﴿Nor can you make the deaf hear the call﴾**. Ibn Kathir recited "wa-la yasmaʿu al-ṣummu" with a fatḥa on the mim of "yasmaʿu" and a ḍamma on the mim of "al-ṣumm".

Allah the Exalted says: **﴿when they turn away, retreating﴾**, meaning: when the deaf turn their backs on you, and you call them, they do not hear, and so it is with the disbeliever. **﴿Nor can you guide the blind away from their error﴾**, meaning: you cannot guide one whom Allah has blinded to guidance. **﴿You can make none hear except those who believe in Our signs﴾**, meaning hearing that brings understanding.

Allah the Exalted says: **﴿And when the word is fulfilled against them, We will bring forth for them a creature from the earth﴾**. "Waqaʿa" here means "wajaba" (became due).

Regarding what is meant by "the word" there are three views:
One: the punishment, said by Ibn ʿAbbas. Two: the anger, said by Qatadah. Three: the proof, said by Ibn Qutaybah.

When does this happen? There are two views:
One: when they do not enjoin what is right and do not forbid what is wrong, said by Ibn ʿUmar and Abu Said al-Khudri.
Two: when there is no hope for their reform, related by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi, and this is the meaning of the statement of Abu al-ʿAliyah. The reference of "them" (ʿalayhim) is to the disbelievers upon whom the creature will emerge.

The commentators have four views on the description of the creature:
One: it has fur and feathers, related by Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Ibn ʿAbbas said: it has down and feathers, and four legs.
Two: its head is that of an ox, its eye that of a pig, its ear that of an elephant, its horn that of a deer, its chest that of a lion, its colour that of a panther, its flank that of a cat, its tail that of a ram, and its legs those of a camel, with twelve cubits between each two joints. This was related by Ibn Jurayj from Abu al-Zubayr.
Three: its face is the face of a man, and the rest of its form is like that of a bird, said by Wahb.
Four: it has four legs, down, feathers and two wings, said by Muqatil.

Regarding the place from which it emerges, there are five views:
One: from al-Safa. Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "While ʿIsa is circumambulating the House with the Muslims, the earth will tremble beneath them, and al-Safa will split on the side facing al-Sa'y, and the creature will come forth from al-Safa. The first thing to appear of it will be its head, shining, with fur and feathers. No seeker will overtake it, and no fleeing one will escape it." In another hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) he said: "Its length is sixty cubits." Likewise Ibn Masʿud said: it emerges from al-Safa. Ibn ʿUmar said: it emerges from a crack in al-Safa, running like a horse for three days, and not even a third of it will have emerged. Abdullah ibn ʿUmar said: the creature emerges, its head touching the clouds while its feet remain in the earth as long as they have not come out.
Two: that it emerges from the valley of Ajyad, related from the Prophet (ﷺ), and similarly from Ibn ʿUmar.
Three: that it emerges from one of the valleys of Tihamah, said by Ibn ʿAbbas.
Four: from the Sea of Sodom, said by Wahb ibn Munabbih.
Five: that it emerges in Tihamah between al-Safa and al-Marwah, related by al-Zajjaj. Abu Hurayrah related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The creature will emerge with the seal of Solomon and the staff of Moses. It will polish the face of the believer with the staff, and strike the nose of the disbeliever with the seal, so much so that the people of a house will gather, and this one will say: 'O believer!' and that one will say: 'O disbeliever!'" It is also related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "It will mark the believer between his eyes and write between his eyes: 'Believer,' and it will mark the disbeliever between his eyes and write between his eyes: 'Disbeliever.' It will cry out three cries that will be heard between the two horizons." Ḥudhayfah ibn Usayd said: the creature has three emergences: one emergence in some of the deserts, then it vanishes; and one emergence in some of the villages, then it vanishes. Then while people are at the most noble of the mosques, meaning al-Masjid al-Ḥaram, the earth will rise, and the people will flee in terror, but they will not escape it. It will even reach a man while he is praying, and we will say: "Do you seek refuge in prayer? By Allah, you were never one of the people of prayer!" Then it will strike him on the nose, and polish the face of the believer. Abdullah ibn ʿAmr said: it will mark the face of the disbeliever with a black spot which spreads over his face until his face turns black, and it will mark the face of the believer with a white spot which spreads over his face until his face turns white, so that people will recognise the believer and the disbeliever. "It is as if I can see it having emerged in the wake of a caravan of pilgrims."

Allah the Exalted says: **﴿speaks to them﴾**. Most readers recited it with a shadda on the lam, so it is from speech (kalam).

Regarding what it says to them, there are three views:
One: it says to them: "The people did not have certainty in Our signs," said by Qatadah.
Two: it speaks to them about the falsehood of all religions other than the religion of Islam, said by al-Suddi.
Three: it says: "This one is a believer, and this one is a disbeliever," related by al-Mawardi.

Ibn Abi ʿAblah and al-Jahdari recited it with a sukun on the kaf and a kasra on the lam [and a fatḥa on the ta'], so it is from "kalm" (wounding). Thaʿlab said: the meaning is: it wounds them. Ibn ʿAbbas was asked about the two readings and said: "Both of them, by Allah, it does: the believer speaks, and the wicked and disbeliever speak," meaning: it wounds him.

Allah the Exalted says: **﴿that the people﴾**. ʿAsim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited it with a fatḥa on the hamzah, and the rest recited it with a kasra. Whoever read it with a fatḥa meant: it speaks to them about the fact that the people (…). Likewise Ibn Masʿud and Abu ʿImran al-Jawni recited: "tukallimuhum bi-anna al-nās," with an added bāʾ and a fatḥa on the hamzah. Whoever read it with a kasra, then because the meaning of "tukallimuhum" is: it says to them, "Indeed the people," and speech is a saying.

(p-194) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [mention] the Day when We will gather from every nation a company (fawj)﴾. The fawj is a group of people, like a troop (zumrah). What is meant by it is the leaders and those who were followed in disbelief. They are gathered, and the proof is established against them. The meaning of ﴿they are driven on (yuza'un)﴾ has already passed [in Surah An-Naml 17]. ﴿Until, when they have come﴾ to the place of reckoning, God, exalted is He, says to them: ﴿Did you deny My verses?﴾ This is a question of rebuke against them and a threat to them. ﴿While you did not encompass them in knowledge﴾ — concerning this there are two opinions.

One of them: you did not know them with true knowledge.

The second: you did not comprehend with knowledge their falsehood. The meaning is: you did not reflect on their truth. ﴿Then what was it you used to do?﴾ in the world, regarding what I commanded you and forbade you from?

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the word will fall upon them﴾ — we have already explained it a little earlier [An-Naml 82]. ﴿For what they wronged﴾, that is, for what they associated [with God]. ﴿So they will not speak﴾ with any argument on their own behalf. Then He argued against them with the verse that follows this one. And the meaning of His saying, ﴿and the day giving sight (mubsiran)﴾ is that one sees in it while seeking provision.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 27, verses 87–90:**

The words of the Most High: ﴿And on the Day when the Horn is blown﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "This is the first blast."

The words of the Most High: ﴿so whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified﴾. [The exegetes (al-mufassirun) said: the meaning is: so whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified.] What is meant is that they die; the terror reaches the point of death.

Regarding His words: ﴿except whom Allah wills﴾, there are three opinions.

The first: they are the martyrs. This was said by Abu Hurayra, Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The second: they are Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil, and the Angel of Death. Then Allah Most High will cause them to die after that. This was said by Muqatil.

The third: they are those in Paradise among the houris and others, and likewise those in the Fire, because they were created for permanence. This was mentioned by Abu Ishaq ibn Shaqila from among our companions.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And all will come to Him﴾, meaning: of the living who died and were then brought back to life, ﴿will come to Him﴾. Hamza and Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, recited ﴿atawhu﴾ with a fatha on the ta' and without the madd (ʾatawhu), meaning: they come to Allah on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿humbled﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatada said: "humbled," meaning abased. Abu 'Ubayda said: "kull" (all) is grammatically singular in form, but its meaning falls upon the plural, so this verse is in the place of a plural.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And you see the mountains﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: This will be when the Horn is blown; the mountains will be gathered and set in motion. Because of their vastness, ﴿you think them fixed﴾, meaning standing still, ﴿while they pass by﴾, meaning they move like the passing of clouds. Likewise, every great army appears to the observer from afar as standing still while it is moving, because of its vastness. Al-Ja'di, describing an army, said:

"With a mass like a mountain, you think they are standing still for pilgrims, while the riding camels trot along."

The words of the Most High: ﴿the handiwork of Allah﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), because His words ﴿And you see the mountains, you think them fixed, while they pass by﴾ indicate the act of making. It is as if He said: "Allah made that as a making." It is also permissible to read it in the nominative, with the meaning: "that is the handiwork of Allah." As for ﴿itqan﴾ (perfection), in the language it means the making of a thing firm and sound.

The words of the Most High: ﴿Indeed, He is Acquainted with what you do﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿ya'maluna﴾ with the ya' (they do). Nafi', 'Asim, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read it with the ta' (you do).

The words of the Most High: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed﴾. We have already explained the good deed and the evil deed at the end of al-An'am (6:160).

The words of the Most High: ﴿he will have better than it﴾. There are two opinions regarding this.

The first: he will have something better than it that reaches him, which is the reward. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and 'Ikrima.

The second: he will have something better than it, because he brings one good deed and is given ten times its like. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And they will be safe from terror that Day﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿min fazaʿi yawmiʾidh﴾ with the noun in the genitive construct (idafa), "from the terror of that Day." 'Asim, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read ﴿min fazaʿin﴾ with tanwin (nunation) and ﴿yawmaʾidhin﴾ with a fatha on the mim. Al-Farra' said: the idafa is more pleasing to me in Arabic, because it is a known terror; do you not see His words: ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾ (21:103), where He made it definite (ma'rifa). So when you add to the definite, it is more beloved to me. Abu 'Ubayda preferred the reading with tanwin and said: it is the more general of the two interpretations, so that safety is from all the terror of that Day. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: when it is read with tanwin, it is permissible that it means one terror, and it is permissible that it means multiplicity, because it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and verbal nouns indicate multiplicity even if their wording is singular, as in His words: ﴿Indeed, the most hideous of voices is the braying of donkeys﴾ (31:19). Likewise, when it is in the idafa construction, it is permissible that it means one terror and permissible that it means multiplicity. According to this view, the two readings are equal. If multiplicity is intended, it encompasses every terror that will occur on the Day of Resurrection; if one terror is intended, it is the one referred to by His words: ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾ (21:103). Ibn al-Sa'ib said: when the Fire closes over its people, they will be terrified with a terror the like of which they have never known, while the people of Paradise will be safe from that terror.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed﴾. The exegetes said: it is shirk (associating partners with Allah). ﴿Their faces will be overturned﴾. It is said: "I overturned (kabbabtu) the man" when I cast him onto his face. And the keepers of Hell will say to them: ﴿Are you recompensed except for what you used to do?﴾, meaning: only the recompense of what you used to do in the world of shirk.

The words of the Most High: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed﴾. We have already explained the good deed and the evil deed at the end of al-An'am (6:160).

The words of the Most High: ﴿he will have better than it﴾. There are two opinions regarding this.

The first: he will have something better than it that reaches him, which is the reward. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and 'Ikrima.

The second: he will have something better than it, because he brings one good deed and is given ten times its like. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And they will be safe from terror that Day﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿min fazaʿi yawmiʾidh﴾ with the noun in the genitive construct (idafa), "from the terror of that Day." 'Asim, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read ﴿min fazaʿin﴾ with tanwin (nunation) and ﴿yawmaʾidhin﴾ with a fatha on the mim. Al-Farra' said: the idafa is more pleasing to me in Arabic, because it is a known terror; do you not see His words: ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾ (21:103), where He made it definite (ma'rifa). So when you add to the definite, it is more beloved to me. Abu 'Ubayda preferred the reading with tanwin and said: it is the more general of the two interpretations, so that safety is from all the terror of that Day. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: when it is read with tanwin, it is permissible that it means one terror, and it is permissible that it means multiplicity, because it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and verbal nouns indicate multiplicity even if their wording is singular, as in His words: ﴿Indeed, the most hideous of voices is the braying of donkeys﴾ (31:19). Likewise, when it is in the idafa construction, it is permissible that it means one terror and permissible that it means multiplicity. According to this view, the two readings are equal. If multiplicity is intended, it encompasses every terror that will occur on the Day of Resurrection; if one terror is intended, it is the one referred to by His words: ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾ (21:103). Ibn al-Sa'ib said: when the Fire closes over its people, they will be terrified with a terror the like of which they have never known, while the people of Paradise will be safe from that terror.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed﴾. The exegetes said: it is shirk (associating partners with Allah). ﴿Their faces will be overturned﴾. It is said: "I overturned (kabbabtu) the man" when I cast him onto his face. And the keepers of Hell will say to them: ﴿Are you recompensed except for what you used to do?﴾, meaning: only the recompense of what you used to do in the world of shirk.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 27, verses 87–90:**

The words of the Most High: ﴿And on the Day when the Horn is blown﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "This is the first blast."

The words of the Most High: ﴿so whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified﴾. [The exegetes (al-mufassirun) said: the meaning is: so whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified.] What is meant is that they die; the terror reaches the point of death.

Regarding His words: ﴿except whom Allah wills﴾, there are three opinions.

The first: they are the martyrs. This was said by Abu Hurayra, Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The second: they are Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil, and the Angel of Death. Then Allah Most High will cause them to die after that. This was said by Muqatil.

The third: they are those in Paradise among the houris and others, and likewise those in the Fire, because they were created for permanence. This was mentioned by Abu Ishaq ibn Shaqila from among our companions.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And all will come to Him﴾, meaning: of the living who died and were then brought back to life, ﴿will come to Him﴾. Hamza and Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, recited ﴿atawhu﴾ with a fatha on the ta' and without the madd (ʾatawhu), meaning: they come to Allah on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿humbled﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatada said: "humbled," meaning abased. Abu 'Ubayda said: "kull" (all) is grammatically singular in form, but its meaning falls upon the plural, so this verse is in the place of a plural.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And you see the mountains﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: This will be when the Horn is blown; the mountains will be gathered and set in motion. Because of their vastness, ﴿you think them fixed﴾, meaning standing still, ﴿while they pass by﴾, meaning they move like the passing of clouds. Likewise, every great army appears to the observer from afar as standing still while it is moving, because of its vastness. Al-Ja'di, describing an army, said:

"With a mass like a mountain, you think they are standing still for pilgrims, while the riding camels trot along."

The words of the Most High: ﴿the handiwork of Allah﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), because His words ﴿And you see the mountains, you think them fixed, while they pass by﴾ indicate the act of making. It is as if He said: "Allah made that as a making." It is also permissible to read it in the nominative, with the meaning: "that is the handiwork of Allah." As for ﴿itqan﴾ (perfection), in the language it means the making of a thing firm and sound.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 27, verses 91–93:

(p-198) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, who has made it sacred﴾. The meaning: Say to the polytheists, "Indeed, I have only been commanded ﴿to worship the Lord of this city, who has made it sacred﴾." Ibn Mas'ud and Abu 'Imran al-Jawni recited, "al-latee harramaha" (the feminine form, "the one which He has made sacred"). It refers to Makkah, and its being made sacred means magnifying its sanctity by prohibiting killing within it, taking captives, and refraining from hunting its game and cutting its trees. ﴿And to Him belongs everything﴾, because He is its Creator and Owner. ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾, i.e., among those who are sincere to God in monotheism. ﴿And to recite the Qur'an﴾ to you. ﴿So whoever is guided, he is only guided for his own soul﴾, i.e., for him is the reward of his guidance. ﴿And whoever goes astray﴾, i.e., errs from [the path of] guidance, ﴿then say, "I am only among the warners"﴾, i.e., there is upon me only the conveyance (of the message). The exegetes mention that this is abrogated by the verse of the sword (naskh, abrogation, a technical term meaning the replacement of a ruling by a later one). ﴿And say, "Praise be to God"﴾, i.e., say to those who have gone astray, "Praise be to God, who has enabled us to accept what you have refused." ﴿He will show you His signs, and you will recognize them﴾.

Regarding when He will show them, there are two opinions.

The first: in this world. Then there are three sayings concerning it. One: that among them are the smoke and the splitting of the moon, and He has shown them that, narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: "He will show you His signs" [and you will recognize them] in the heavens, in yourselves, and in provision, as said by Mujahid. The third: the killing at Badr, as said by Muqatil.

The second: "He will show you His signs" in the Hereafter, and you will recognize them as they were described in this world, as said by al-Hasan.

(p-199) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what you do﴾. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs from 'Asim recited "ta'lamun" with a *ta'* (second person, "you do"), meaning: say to them. The rest recited it with a *ya'* (third person, "they do"), meaning it is a warning to them of recompense for their deeds.
